posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: Visually seeing air movement around table.
posts.content_md:
Michael's "get away from the table" reminded me of this trick.

To visually see if you have air currents around your table, take a few feathers and tie them to thin pieces of thread (quill end). Then hang them over your table. They will easily move with the least bit of air movement.

[quote:1c4b96a8b7="JohnFP"]Michael's "get away from the table" reminded me of this trick.

To visually see if you have air currents around your table, take a few feathers and tie them to thin pieces of thread (quill end). Then hang them over your table. They will easily move with the least bit of air movement.[/quote:1c4b96a8b7]

Easily? What if the air is too gentle to cause the feathers to move. Or if the inertia of the feathers is too large to cause motion? If the feathers don't move, can you assume there are no air currents? If the feathers do move (say from a stray draft or someone opening a door) won't the inertia keep the feathers moving and creating it's own air currents? Also, I assume you'd need to have some sort of structure above your table to hang them from? It seems a little elaborate to build a structure to hang feathers but have them accesible so as to stop them moving if a stray air current starts them off. It seems a lot simpler just to put a screen around the table if you're worried about air currents.

[quote:fc2c95af83="MichaelH"][quote:fc2c95af83="Dinesh"]...[/quote:fc2c95af83]

You're joking, right?[/quote:fc2c95af83]

No, I'm not. This is one of those clever, theoretical techniques that's stated just to show how clever the proposer is but has no value as a serious tip.It needs to be tried as a useful technique. It's alweays possile to hang a bunch of feathers and watch as one (invariably) moves but such a test is useless unless there's a correlation between movement-of-feather and brightness-of-hologram.. I believe that feathers floating above the table will create a bigger problem than they attempt to solve. Why tha added weight of the feathers? Why not just a cotton ball. A feather presents a large surface area, especially with all those "hairs", for lack of a better term. This presents a lot of inertia. Once moving, for whatever reason, they'll keep moving and so you'd need to keep leaning over the table and steadying them.

 How much air movement are we trying to measure? Maybe someone can actually take a feather and hold it up in average room with the windows closed and try to establish that it'll detect air velocity sufficent to move an object by roughly 200 nm. To move a mass of air sufficently to overcome the inertia of a fairly massive optical mount and then cause it to move by 200nm will never be seenas movement of a feather by the naked eye. If there's enough of an airflow to actually see a feather moving, I suggest there's a lot more problems with your table. 

I know there are people here who stand up and cry Hallelujah! every time a John idea is stated. Any critical analysis of that idea seems to be frowned upon and attacked. However, I maintain that the velocity of air needed to detect motion down to 315nm (for HeNe) will not be detected by a feather. If this is a serious "tip" then anyone should be allowed to criticise it. Any criticism should be then evaluated on the basis of that criticism. Not hyperbole and invective.

[quote:fc2c95af83="JohnFP"]OMG!!!

Dude, it's a feather and string held to the ceiling with a thumb tack or something. Not a $100,000 air particle tracker. I know the complexity of it would require just a little bit of common sense in realizing what it shows but I didn't think and instruction manual and a calibration tutorial was necessary.[/quote:fc2c95af83]

You've suggested this as a tip for holography. Therefore you believe it's a useful technique for holographers. I've evaluated the idea, based on some knowledge of physics and holography, and I've found that it has some serious problems as a tip. Hyperbole is not a useful method as an evaluation of the criticisms. You can hang pretty much anything you like from the ceiling. You can hang a CD player from the ceiling with a torsion balance such that any movement starts the CD and plays a CD of the St Paul's Choir singing the Hallelujah Chorus. I'm sure you're fans will attack me for this hyperbole while allowing all your hyperbole, however.

Sadly, critical thinking and rationality has been displaced by a cult of hero-worship

posts.post_subject: Visually seeing air movement around table.
posts.content_md:
I don't know. A feather is designed by God to capture the wind. It is hollow and light (low inertia), has large surface area and is designed with a curve to give lift in one direction it moves very easy. I never understood the thingy about it keep moving, without air currents? Is that like perpetual motion? The pendulum that never slows?

The funny thing is I actually took this criticism as a complement because I have done this in the past and it does work surprisingly well. I used it when I had to put the heat on. After the heat went off and the feather stoped moving violently I knew I had a better atmosphere for a hologram then when the it was moving violently. Since I do single beam hologram should I baffel in between the plate and the object? It was not theory but something I use in the past that helped get brighter holograms by giving me some sort of base line for when the air movement slowed. Was it a calibrated absolute measurement? Well, hopefull I do not have to answer that. And absolutely not, I never noticed the feather itself causing air currents from some perpetual inertial motion after the force that acted upon it stopped. If the air stopped they barely moved. Perfectly still? Not sure I never waited that long. When then slowed it was better, very simple.

Of course boxing off your entire table would be better for some but for a few pennies the feather give you a sense of what is going on.

All I can say is if you haven't tried it don't knock it's usefullness for the buck or should I say penny.

Maybe someone whom is interested in the physics of the feather would not mind doing some actual tests with data to support or disprove what I have spoken.

Also, in the past, when I've suggested an idea is not practical, the post goes on and on with variations and variations on variations and statements I don't understand such as "do I have a c now" or some such.

It all depends on how you use this feather. If you have a fairly strong source of wind currents (such as a heater) and you want to know how long you can wait after turning it off, this is one way. It's a pretty elaborate way and there are much easier methods, but it's one way. However if you wanted to know how the everyday status of the air currents were over your table, with no evidently strong source of wind. Then this will not give you the results you want. Random air currents sufficent to cause motion of 200 nm (about the size of a large protein molecule) will not be strong enough to move a feather. A cobweb, possibly. Even sprinkling talcum powder into an expanded laser beam. 

If John's method is to discover strong wind sources, it'll work. Strong wind sources will be too strong for cobwebs or talcum powder. The implication I got from this was a method of discovering subtle and random air currents from natural sources that occur even when a room appears "still". In this case, a feather has too much mass. It may have been god's way of warning of hurricanes but god does not appear to have understood the difference between 200nm and a cm or so
